title: Variables and scope
notional_machine: A declaration creates a binding: a name attached to a value in one scope. let and const belong to the nearest enclosing block { } and cannot be read before their line runs; var belongs to the whole enclosing function (or module) and starts out as undefined. A name is looked up in the nearest scope first, then outward, and const stops the name being reassigned without freezing the value it holds.
steps: let x = 'outer' creates a binding named x in the module scope.
The if block opens a new scope. let x = 'inner' creates a second, separate x that shadows the outer one only inside the block.
var y ignores the block: it is created in the enclosing function (here the module), so it outlives the block.
After the block, looking up x finds the outer binding again and y is still visible, so it logs outer function-wide.

title: Closures
notional_machine: A function keeps a live reference to the variables in scope where it was created, not a copy of their values. var is scoped to the whole function, so every closure made in a var loop shares one i; let makes a fresh i for each iteration.
steps: makeGreeter('Hi') runs and creates a local variable greeting = 'Hi'.
It returns the arrow function, which keeps a reference to greeting after makeGreeter returns.
hi('Ada') runs the arrow function. greeting is still 'Hi', so it returns 'Hi, Ada'.

title: Array iteration
notional_machine: for...of walks an array by index. Removing elements during the walk shifts later elements left, so the loop skips whichever element moves into the current index. map builds a new array and leaves the original alone.
steps: map calls the arrow function once per element, in order: 10, 20, 30.
Each return value goes into a new array at the same index.
prices is never modified, so it still has 3 elements.

title: Off-by-one bounds
notional_machine: An array of length n has indexes 0 to n - 1. A loop starting at 0 should continue while i < n; i <= n runs one extra time and reads xs[n], which is undefined.
steps: xs.length is 3, so the valid indexes are 0, 1, and 2.
The loop runs while i < 3, so i takes the values 0, 1, 2.
When i becomes 3 the condition is false and the loop stops before reading xs[3].
